title: Hest Foamy Review: Front Country Comfort – Paul Kalifatidi
content:
Paul has spent countless nights sleeping in cars, and he’s got opinions. Those opinions eventually led him to Hest, a Seattle-based company specializing in modern bedroll mattresses. For the past many months, he’s been sleeping comfortably, and now he wants to tell you all about it.

Durable Decision

I imagine that most people who have ever used a sleeping pad have used an inflatable pad. It is the industry standard, and for good reasons: lightweight, packable, and customizable in its firmness. There are a myriad of inflatable pads out there at all price points. Some options are luxuriously plush and comfortable; some are bare-bones and pack as small as a bike bottle. Your mileage may vary as to how comfortable you find any sleeping pad. I have an ultralight Therm-a-Rest that I love for any adventure beyond the reach of a vehicle. My mother swears by her plush Big Agnes that strikes a middle ground between car camping and ultralight backcountry packability. But I have one gigantic gripe with all inflatable sleeping pads: they will, with use, leak and need to be patched.

Growing up, just about every summer weekend was spent camping at Devils Lake with my dad, my brother, and the Chicago Mountaineering Club. My dad is the kind of guy who likes a ridiculously firm mattress. At home, jumping on his side of the bed was a painful experience, as he quite literally had a sheet of plywood on top of the mattress and under the mattress cover. It might come as no surprise then that we did not use inflatable pads while camping and all of us exclusively used Therm-a-Rest Z-Lite foam pads. It wasn’t until I got into bike camping and backpacking, where packability became a concern, that I purchased an inflatable pad, and I’m still on the fence about them. I’ve owned a few over the years, and have always found them to leak and be frustrating. Even when I lived in a Honda Element for a summer, I used two thin foam sleeping pads instead of an inflatable pad or mattress.

Four years ago, I bought my KZJ95 Prado and immediately built a sleeping platform in it. I found an inflatable pad that perfectly fit the shape, and for a long time I loved that setup. And then, a leak. I loved that pad; I found it incredibly comfortable, but after falling asleep on an inflated pad, I would wake up an hour later and feel the hard, cold bed platform underneath me. No longer was good sleep reliable.

Before you jump down my throat about finding the leak and fixing it, trust me, I tried. Most of my possessions are patched and repaired; this sleeping pad was no different. I did find where the leak was, but it was underneath a layer of foam that I had to dig through. After many failed attempts to patch the hole, I used the pad to protect a bicycle that I was shipping, told the new owner they could use it as a dog bed or to use it again to protect a bike, and I switched to a Hest mattress.

Ultimately, the thing that made me reach out to Hest about reviewing their product was wanting a foolproof and leakproof landing pad after a long day of riding, running, or fishing.

Hest Foamy Overview

Camping should not be complicated. Whether you’re sleeping in the car, next to the car, or miles from any cars, you shouldn’t be missing out on sleep. I did not always sleep well when camping, but I have made small changes that have made a monumental difference to the quality of sleep that I get while on the go. Those being, switching from a mummy-style sleeping bag to a quilt when in the backcountry or a big blanket when car camping, and choosing reliability over packability. This article will pertain to reliability and comfort, as you cannot sleep well if you are waking up constantly to inflate a mattress.

The Hest Foamy is dead simple: it’s two densities of memory foam wrapped in a weather-resistant and washable cover. The bottom is covered in a durable and water-resistant PVC-like fabric, while the top, the part your body rests on, is a very comfortable and stretchy fabric. The mattress rolls up, has a carry handle, a small pocket for essentials, and can be attached to a neighboring pad to double the sleeping area. Boom. That’s basically it. There aren’t a ton of features to discuss, and yet, below are 1000 words about why I’ve come to love this piece of gear. Let’s get into it.

 

Hest Foamy Quick Hits

  • Foam core: Two layers of foam provide body contouring support and pressure-point relief. The temperature-resilient foam is designed to perform in cold conditions and is CertiPUR-US certified, meaning it has been made without harsh chemicals and with environmentally friendlier methods.
  • R-value 8.8: High insulation helps keep you warm in colder camping conditions.
  • Outdoor-ready construction: Waterproof, dirt-resistant materials and a waterproof lower fabric help protect you and the mattress from wet, muddy conditions.
  • Compact roll design: Rolls tightly for easy transport and storage, with an integrated compression harness to keep it securely packed. The compression harness doubles as a dry, flat surface for changing clothes when the mattress is unrolled.
  • Easy to carry: A durable built-in handle makes grab-and-go transport simple.
  • Removable, washable cover: Easily remove the cover and machine wash it when needed.
  • Convenient features: A built-in phone pocket keeps small essentials close, while side clips allow you to link mattresses for extra sleeping space.
  • 3 sizes:
    • Foamy Short 64” x 25” x 3.9” (reviewed)
    • Foamy 78″ x 25″ x 3.9”
    • Foamy Wide is 78″ x 30″ x 3.9”
  • $279-379 USD

About Hest

The name Hest is derived from Hestia, the Greek goddess of hearth and home. Hest’s driving goal is to make camping as comfortable as sleeping at home. I see this in the way that they approach their product category: front-country and car camping comfort.

Hest approached this product category differently than most of their competitors, which tend to be heritage camping brands. Those companies have taken their inflatable camping pads, initially meant to be light and packable, and made them larger and more comfortable to bring them back to the front-country. Hest took the at-home mattress idea and slimmed it down to a more packable form factor that I think better solves the comfort side of front-country camping. Removing the inflatable element comes with very minor drawbacks, with the added advantage of foolproof and durable reliability.

Choosing your Hest

There are a myriad of options if you peruse the Hest website. This is a review of two Foamy Short mattresses. When I was initially in discussion with Hest about this review, we were set on the Dually, their fold-in-half mattress meant for one or two people. At the last minute, I decided to switch to two Foamy mattresses instead of the single Dually for two reasons: the Foamy is more adaptable with its waterproof base fabric, and I don’t always need 50″ in width like on long trips where I have duffel bags and gear that occupy half of my sleeping platform.

In hindsight, I think I would have preferred the Dually in the Short size, as it would’ve worked in my Prado and I wouldn’t have experienced one issue that I’ll discuss below. I also did not find myself sleeping on the ground as much as I originally anticipated. But I’m not unhappy with the Foamy options, and I think they are more applicable to more people. Regardless, here’s a brief overview of their mattress options, which are all built using the same fundamental memory foam interior.

  • Foamy: waterproof base, single-person size that can be linked to another mattress, adaptable
  • Dually: folds in half for storage, wide enough for two people, less durable but not really meant to be used outside of a vehicle, comes in a multitude of sizes for RTTs, Rivians, GFC campers, etc.
  • Sleep System: an oddball hybrid option that combines the bread-and-butter Hest Mattress with an inflatable base pad. It’s aimed at frontcountry tent and car camping, but not really meant to be carried deep into the backcountry

Sweet Dreams

I sleep really well on this mattress. It is not a complicated product; there isn’t any trick that unlocks some new level of performance. The face fabric, even without a fitted sheet (which Hest does sell), is very comfortable, even on bare skin. Sometimes, when sleeping on an inflatable pad that feels rather plastic-like, it can get a little clammy. The face fabric and interior foam of the Hest solve this completely; I never felt sweaty because of the mattress. I also have not yet found the need to fully wash the covers. I’ve wiped them down heavily with a wet towel, but they still feel as good as the day I received them. The fabric is not as absorbent as cotton and doesn’t feel like it gets dirty as quickly. Regardless, the washable covers are a welcome change compared to having to soap and spray down my previous sleeping pad.

The Foamy is also quiet. There isn’t any crinkling when rolling around. Now that I’m writing this, I’m curious how often I’ve been unknowingly woken up by a crinkly inflatable pad. I can say that most nights on the Hest were uninterrupted sleeps from beginning to end. I felt well rested for whatever the next day had in store. Speaking of which, the small pockets at the head (or foot) of the mattress are secure and easy-to-access spots for my phone, alarm clock, and wallet. Those are all things that I like having in easy-to-reach and secure places that are also not super visible, should I forget to take them with me the next day.

The compression straps, which double as a welcome mat, have also proved handy. I do wish they were larger, but they are sufficiently big as a place to step when removing shoes. I would miss them if they didn’t exist.

It’s not all sweet dreams.

I do have a few small things I would change to the Foamy if given the opportunity, and indeed, I might bust out a needle and thread and do some experimenting. First on my list of fixes would be the joining mechanism to attach a neighboring pad. Though the two clips work, they do occasionally slide apart. The bigger issue is that they don’t tightly sandwich the two pads together. If you roll into the crack, it is noticeable. While I don’t think couples will have this issue so long as each partner sticks to their own pad, I did find it to be an occasional and minor annoyance when using both pads by myself, which was actually the most common configuration I used.

There are some other sleeping pads on the market that do a better job of this; they feature a closure mechanism in the middle, on the corners, and at all locations, a closure on the top layer and bottom layer. This prevents any gap from opening. The Hest Foamy just has two clips that meet halfway up the foam layer. I’m going to try stitching a layer of hook-and-loop closure to the bottom edge of the pad with a removable strip to prevent the pads from separating. I understand why that isn’t an OEM option, as I don’t think it would be the cleanest-looking solution.

I am 70″ tall and find the Foamy Short to be sufficiently long, as I don’t sleep fully extended like a fishing pole; I curl up a little bit like a human. Yet, I don’t fully understand why there is not a 72″ long Foamy option. The standard Foamy is 78″ long. The Foamy Short is 64″ long. The bed platform that I built in my Prado is 72″ long, or 6′. A Toyota Tacoma (somewhat of a litmus test for car/truck focused camping accessories) has a 5-foot or 6-foot bed length, neither of which matches a Hest Foamy very well. The Dually does come in a 72″x60″ size, but that wouldn’t fit in my Prado. Anyways, this isn’t an issue with the product as much as it is a product strategy decision that is beyond my pay grade and outside of my control.

My final gripe is purely subjective: I would love it if these were slightly firmer. I love a very firm mattress. While the plush feel of the Foamy is still very comfortable and helps me sleep like a baby, the conscious version of me that initially lays down always thinks: perhaps firmer? This is the biggest drawback of not having the customizable firmness of an inflatable pad.

Pillow Talk

I have not yet mentioned it and I absolutely should: the Hest Pillows are amazing. They sent me two for this review, and I didn’t think I would love them so much. They are made out of the same outer materials as the mattress but with a different construction. Instead of layers of foam, the filling is shredded foam. You can remove this filling to achieve whatever level of plumpness that your head desires. I did not remove any as I find the stock level to be perfectly comfortable.

The pillow can be turned inside out when not in use to keep it clean, so when it comes time to put your head on it, the interior becomes the outside, and it is the same face fabric as the surface of the mattress. The cover is also removable for washing, like the mattress. I wholeheartedly recommend these pillows, even if you already have a stellar mattress solution in your rig. I’ve even used them at home; I like them so much.

TL;DR

The Hest Foamy is a great solution for camping settings where packability is not a concern. The memory foam construction doesn’t deflate throughout the night but is supportive and comfortable. The face fabrics are durable and comfortable, and can be removed for washing. The pillows, made out of much of the same materials, are just as wonderful. Overall, if you are looking for a car camping setup, I highly recommend perusing the various mattress and pillow options from Hest.

Pros

  • Reliable Comfort that always supported a good night’s sleep
  • Easy-to-live-with features make ownership easy
  • Feels like a premium bedding option in a setting where most people might expect the bare bones

Cons

  • Pad connectors are finicky
  • The size option you most desire might not exist, but there are also tons to choose from
  • Price might dissuade some buyers
